docDocsGuidesMultiagent.title: Multi-Agent Coordination
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.lead: Run multiple Claude instances on the same project with shared context, task distribution, file locking, a conversational Planning Agent, and an automated Runner Agent for sprint monitoring.
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.overviewPara1: ClaudeNest's multi-agent system lets you run several Claude Code instances that collaborate on a single codebase. Each instance can claim tasks, share context, and lock files to avoid conflicting edits. The coordination happens through a central shared project that acts as the source of truth.
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.overviewPara2: A typical multi-agent workflow looks like this:
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.overviewStep1: Create a shared project on a machine
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.overviewStep2: Define epics grouping related features and create a sprint
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.overviewStep3: Use the Planning Agent to decompose epics into tasks with story points
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.overviewStep5: Each instance claims a task (files are auto-locked), and works
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.overviewStep6: The Runner Agent monitors progress and auto-updates task statuses
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.overviewStep7: On completion, context is stored for other instances to query via RAG
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.overviewTip: Multi-agent coordination is entirely optional. You can use ClaudeNest with a single session and no shared project at all.
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.sharedProjectsPara1: A shared project is the central hub that links instances, tasks, context chunks, and file locks together. It stores high-level metadata such as a project summary, architecture notes, coding conventions, and the current development focus.
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.creatingSharedProjectPara: The response includes the new project ID that you will use for all subsequent multi-agent operations.
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.updatingProjectContextPara: Keep the shared context up to date so every instance has the latest information about conventions, focus areas, and recent changes.
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.instancesPara1: A Claude instance represents one running Claude Code process that is connected to a shared project. Instances are registered automatically when an agent connects, but you can also list and inspect them via the API.
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.instancesStatusPara: Each instance exposes its current status (active, idle, busy, or disconnected), the task it is working on, and its token usage.
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.coordinationPara1: The task system is the primary mechanism for distributing work across instances. Tasks support priorities, dependencies, and atomic claiming to guarantee that no two instances work on the same task simultaneously.
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.claimingTaskPara: An instance claims a task atomically. If the task is already claimed or its dependencies are not met, the server returns an error.
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.completingTaskPara: When the work is done, the instance marks the task as completed. A context chunk is automatically created from the completion summary so other instances can learn from it.
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.coordinationTip: Use GET /projects/{id}/tasks/next-available to let the server pick the highest-priority task whose dependencies are all satisfied.
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.planningAgentPara1: The Planning Agent is a conversational AI interface that helps you decompose work, assign story points, and populate sprints. Access it via a chat-style API or from the web dashboard's Planning tab.
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.howItWorksStep1: The agent analyses your current backlog, velocity history, and epic structure
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.howItWorksStep2: You ask it to break down features, estimate work, or suggest sprint scope
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.howItWorksStep3: It returns structured suggestions (create tasks, assign points, group into epics)
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.howItWorksStep4: You approve or modify the suggestions before they are applied
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.planningAgentTip: Sprint & velocity tracking — story points, burndown data and velocity stats ready for sprint planning.
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.runnerAgentPara1: The Runner Agent is an automated monitoring service that runs in the background and keeps your project dashboard in sync. It watches Claude instance activity and automatically updates task statuses.
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.capability1: Auto-status updates — Detects when an instance finishes a task and marks it as done
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.capability2: Stale task alerts — Flags tasks that have been in-progress for too long without activity
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.capability3: Sprint progress tracking — Provides live burndown data and on-track/off-track indicators
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.capability4: Blocked task detection — Identifies tasks whose dependencies are stuck
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.enhancedFileLockingPara1: File locking in ClaudeNest v1.2 includes several improvements over basic locks:
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.lockingFeature2: Task-lock integration — Files listed in a task's files array are automatically locked when the task is claimed and released when completed
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.lockingFeature3: Heartbeat auto-extend — Locks are automatically extended as long as the agent session is alive, preventing mid-task expiration
docDocsGuidesMultiagent.lockingFeature4: Batch conflict check via POST /locks/conflicts — Check multiple files in a single request before starting a large task

docDocsGuidesRagpipeline.title: RAG Pipeline
docDocsGuidesRagpipeline.lead: Context retrieval augmented generation with pgvector. Share knowledge across Claude instances so every agent benefits from work already done.
docDocsGuidesRagpipeline.howItWorksPara1: The RAG pipeline turns free-text context into searchable vector embeddings stored in PostgreSQL via the pgvector extension. When an instance needs information, the server converts the query into an embedding and finds the most relevant chunks using cosine similarity.
docDocsGuidesRagpipeline.stepEmbedPre: The content is sent to the embedding model
docDocsGuidesRagpipeline.stepStorePre: The vector and its source text are persisted in the
docDocsGuidesRagpipeline.stepStorePost: table alongside metadata such as the originating instance, related files, and an importance score.
docDocsGuidesRagpipeline.stepSearchPre: At query time the same embedding model converts the question into a vector. An IVFFlat index on the
docDocsGuidesRagpipeline.stepSearchPost: table returns the closest matches by cosine distance.
docDocsGuidesRagpipeline.stepCompileText: The top-k results are assembled into a context payload that the requesting instance can consume directly.
docDocsGuidesRagpipeline.howItWorksTip: If the embedding service (Ollama) is unavailable, the server falls back to keyword-based search so context queries never completely fail.
docDocsGuidesRagpipeline.addingContextPost: . Each chunk is a self-contained piece of knowledge — a task completion summary, an architecture decision, a code review note, etc. The server automatically generates the embedding when the chunk is created.
docDocsGuidesRagpipeline.chunkTypesPost: field to categorize chunks so you can filter them later:
docDocsGuidesRagpipeline.typeTaskCompletion: Summary produced when a task is marked done
docDocsGuidesRagpipeline.typeFileSummary: Condensed description of a file or module
docDocsGuidesRagpipeline.queryingPre: Send a natural-language query and the server returns the most relevant chunks ranked by similarity. You can control how many results are returned with the
docDocsGuidesRagpipeline.similarityPost: score between 0 and 1. Values above 0.8 are usually highly relevant; below 0.5 the match is weak.

docDocsGuidesRagpipeline.embeddingModelPost: served by Ollama for generating embeddings. This model produces 384-dimensional vectors and strikes a good balance between accuracy and speed.

docDocsGuidesRemotesessions.title: Remote Sessions
docDocsGuidesRemotesessions.lead: Create and manage remote Claude Code sessions on your registered machines. Sessions support three modes, real-time WebSocket streaming, and full lifecycle management.
docDocsGuidesRemotesessions.createPara1: To start a Claude Code session, send a POST request to the sessions endpoint with the target machine ID. You can specify a working directory, an initial prompt, and the session mode.
docDocsGuidesRemotesessions.createPara2: The session starts in {created} status, transitions to {starting} while the agent spawns the Claude Code process, and then moves to {running} once the PTY is ready.
docDocsGuidesRemotesessions.createTip: Save the returned session {id} — you will need it to attach, send input, or terminate the session.
docDocsGuidesRemotesessions.interactivePara1: Interactive sessions provide a full bidirectional terminal experience. You send input (keystrokes, commands) and receive real-time output via WebSocket. This is the default mode and is ideal for the web dashboard and mobile apps.
docDocsGuidesRemotesessions.attachPara1: To interact with an interactive session, first request a WebSocket token, then connect to the Reverb WebSocket server:
docDocsGuidesRemotesessions.wsCommPara1: Once attached, use the WebSocket connection to send input and receive output in real time:
docDocsGuidesRemotesessions.wsCommTip: Terminal resize events should be sent whenever the client viewport changes to keep the PTY dimensions in sync with the display.
docDocsGuidesRemotesessions.headlessPara1: Headless sessions run without user interaction. Claude Code executes the initial prompt autonomously and completes when done. This mode is ideal for batch processing, CI/CD pipelines, and automated tasks.
docDocsGuidesRemotesessions.headlessPara2: Headless sessions automatically transition through {created} → {starting} → {running} → {completed} without requiring any further interaction. You can poll the session status or listen to WebSocket events to know when the task finishes.
docDocsGuidesRemotesessions.oneshotPara1: Oneshot sessions execute a single command or prompt and terminate immediately after. They are designed for quick, atomic operations such as code generation, analysis, or one-off queries.
docDocsGuidesRemotesessions.oneshotPara2: Unlike headless mode, oneshot sessions are expected to complete within a short time frame. The response includes any output produced during execution.
docDocsGuidesRemotesessions.oneshotTip: Use oneshot mode for quick tasks that do not require ongoing context. For longer-running autonomous work, prefer headless mode.
docDocsGuidesRemotesessions.monitoringPara1: ClaudeNest provides several ways to monitor session status and review output after the fact.
docDocsGuidesRemotesessions.statusPara1: Query the session endpoint to check its current status, token usage, cost, and duration:
docDocsGuidesRemotesessions.logsPara1: Every session records a complete log of all input and output. Retrieve logs for debugging, auditing, or replaying sessions:
docDocsGuidesRemotesessions.logTypeInput: User input sent to Claude Code
docDocsGuidesRemotesessions.terminatePara1: To stop a running session, send a DELETE request. The agent will send a SIGTERM to the Claude Code process and clean up resources:

docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.lead: Distribute and coordinate work between Claude instances. Tasks provide an atomic claiming system that prevents conflicts and ensures each unit of work is handled by exactly one agent at a time.
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.lifecyclePara1: Every task follows a well-defined lifecycle from creation to completion. Understanding these states is key to building reliable multi-agent workflows.
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.lifecycleBlocked: A task can also enter the {blocked} state if it depends on other tasks that have not yet been completed. Blocked tasks cannot be claimed until all dependencies are resolved.
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.lifecycleTip: If an instance cannot finish a task, it can release it back to {pending} so another instance can pick it up.
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.creatingPara1: Create tasks within a shared project. Each task includes a title, optional description, priority level, and an estimate of the token budget required.
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.creatingResponseIntro: The response returns the newly created task with its {pending} status:
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.claimingPara1: Claiming is an {atomic}: only one instance can claim a given task. If two instances try to claim the same task simultaneously, only one succeeds and the other receives a {conflict} response.
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.claimingSuccessIntro: On success the task status changes to {inProgress}:
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.claimingTakenIntro: If the task is already taken:
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.nextTaskPara1: Instead of choosing a specific task, an instance can request the next available task whose dependencies are satisfied:
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.nextTaskTip: The server picks the highest-priority, oldest-pending task whose dependencies are all in {done} status.
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.completingPara1: When an instance finishes its work it marks the task as {done} and provides a summary. The server automatically creates a context chunk from the completion summary so other instances can benefit from the result via RAG.
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.completingResponseIntro: The response confirms the task is done:
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.releasingPara1: If an instance cannot finish its work, it should release the task so others can pick it up. Provide an optional reason to help the next claimant understand the context:
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.dependenciesPara1: Tasks can declare dependencies on other tasks. A dependent task cannot be claimed until every task it depends on has reached the {done} status.
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.dependenciesPara2: The dependency graph is validated at claim time. If a dependency is still pending or in progress, the server returns a {error400} error:
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.dependenciesTip: Keep dependency chains short. Deep chains slow down parallel execution because later tasks must wait for all predecessors to complete sequentially.
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.epicsSprintsIntro: For larger projects, ClaudeNest extends the basic task model with epics, sprints, and subtasks. These concepts let you structure work at multiple granularity levels and track delivery pace across iterations.
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.epicsPara1: An {epic} is a named group of related tasks that together deliver a single feature or capability. Attach a task to an epic by setting its {epicId} field at creation time or via PATCH:
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.epicsPara2: Retrieve all tasks that belong to a given epic using the {epicIdFilter} filter on the task list endpoint. The Projects API exposes a dedicated {epicsEndpoint} endpoint that returns all epics with their aggregate progress (total tasks, completed tasks, percent done).
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.sprintsPara1: A {sprint} is a time-boxed iteration, typically one to two weeks, that contains a selected set of tasks. Sprints help the team commit to a deliverable scope and measure velocity via a burndown chart. Assign a task to the current sprint with {sprintId}:
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.sprintsPara2: Use {sprintsEndpoint} to list all sprints. Each sprint object includes {startsAt}, {endsAt}, total story points, and completed story points so you can render a burndown without additional queries.
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.subtasksPara1: Any task can be broken down into subtasks by setting {parentId} to the parent task's UUID. Subtasks appear nested under their parent and follow the same lifecycle (pending → in_progress → done). A parent task is considered finished only when all its subtasks are done.
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.subtasksPara2: Fetch all subtasks of a task with {subtasksEndpoint}. To show only root-level tasks (no subtasks) in a list, pass {rootOnly}. The response includes convenience fields: {hasSubtasks}, {subtasksCount}, and {completedSubtasksCount}.
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.storyPointsPara1: Attach a {storyPoints} integer to any task to express its relative complexity. Story points are used by sprint burndown calculations and by the Planning Agent to suggest realistic sprint scopes. Common scales are Fibonacci (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13) or T-shirt sizes mapped to numbers (S=1, M=2, L=3, XL=5).
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.agentsIntro: ClaudeNest ships two built-in automation agents that operate at the project level:
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.planningAgentItem: Sprint & velocity tracking — story points, burndown data and velocity stats ready for sprint planning.
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.runnerAgentItem: Runner health checks — on-demand status updates, stale-task detection and sprint progress metrics.
docDocsGuidesTaskcoordination.agentsTip: Let the Planning Agent propose the sprint scope, then have each Claude instance call {nextAvailable} to claim tasks automatically. The Runner Agent keeps the dashboard in sync without any manual status updates.
